Session 3: Weather API — First Real Requests & Geocoding

Day 2 — 9:00 AM to 10:00 AM

Author

Immanuel Williams

Published

August 6, 2026

Welcome Back — Day 2

Yesterday we built the conceptual foundation:

  • Session 1: JSON structure, request/response flow, status codes
  • Session 2: CRUD framework, GET/POST methods, URL anatomy

Today we apply everything to a real API — the free Open-Meteo weather API. We’ll make authentic requests, handle real responses, and turn them into data frames we can analyze.

Important🎯 The One Goal — Today We Do It

Make a request to an API, then format the response into something we can analyze.

By the end of this hour, you will have done this — for real, in R, with live weather data.

Part 1: Meet the Open-Meteo API

We will use Open-Meteo — a free weather API built for exactly this kind of learning:

  • No sign-up. No API key. No credit card. You can start making requests immediately.
  • The main endpoint is:
request("https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast")

That address — https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast — is the endpoint from Session 2: the stable “front door” that never changes. Everything else we want (which city, which measurements, which units) goes in the query string.

NoteWhy api.open-meteo.com and Not Just open-meteo.com?

Notice the endpoint is not the same address as the regular website. Open-Meteo actually has two front doors:

  • open-meteo.com — the door for humans: a web page with documentation, meant to be read in a browser.
  • api.open-meteo.com — the door for programs: a server whose only job is to answer requests with raw JSON data.

Putting the API on its own api. subdomain is a near-universal convention — it lets the company run, scale, and update the data service separately from the marketing/docs website. When you see api. at the front of a domain, you’re looking at the machine door, not the human one. Keep this in mind: later today we’ll meet a third door for a different service.

NoteWhat About API Keys, Clients & Secrets?

Many commercial APIs (OpenWeather, X, Spotify, …) require you to register and receive credentials — an API key, sometimes a client ID and secret — which you attach to every request like an ID card, and which you must store carefully (never directly in your script!). It’s an important real-world concept, and the Practice Labs on this site show it in action.

But today we get to skip all of it. Open-Meteo is free and open — so we can spend our hour on the actual skill: requests and responses.

Tip🎯 Goal Check

One endpoint, no key, live data. The only thing between us and the goal is building the query string — which you already learned to read yesterday.

———————

Q1.

(Fill in the Blank): The stable part of the URL — https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast — that never changes from one request to the next is called the ________.

TipAnswer Q1

The endpoint. The changing part (after the ?) is the query string.

———————

———————

Q2.

(Multiple Choice): Which statement about the Open-Meteo API is true?

  1. It requires a paid subscription.
  2. It requires an API key stored in .Renviron.
  3. It is free and requires no API key at all.
  4. It only works inside Positron.
  5. It only returns data for cities in Europe.
TipAnswer Q2

c) Open-Meteo is free and open — no key, no registration. (Many other APIs do require a key; that’s the “ID card” concept from the callout above.)

———————

Part 2: See It in the Browser First — The Big Moment

Stop. This is the moment the last two sessions have been building toward.

For a day and a half, “request” and “response” have been arrows on a diagram. In the next sixty seconds they become real — and you will not write a single line of code to do it.

Here is the payoff of Session 2’s URL anatomy: a request is just a URL — so a web browser can make one. Look at this URL before you paste it. You can already read every piece of it — that’s Session 2:

https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=35.28&longitude=-120.66&current=temperature_2m&temperature_unit=fahrenheit
  • https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast — the endpoint (the stable front door)
  • ? — “here come my details”
  • latitude=35.28&longitude=-120.66 — where (San Luis Obispo)
  • current=temperature_2m — what (the temperature right now)
  • temperature_unit=fahrenheit — how (in °F)

You are literally looking at a request, written out as a URL. Now copy it, paste it into a new browser tab, and press Enter.

What just happened? Your browser sent that request across the internet to Open-Meteo’s server, and the server answered. What came back is not a web page — no colors, no buttons, no ads. It is a raw JSON response, exactly the structure we studied in Session 1, sitting right there in your browser:

{
  "latitude": 35.28,
  "longitude": -120.66,
  "timezone": "GMT",
  "current_units": { "time": "iso8601", "temperature_2m": "°F" },
  "current": {
    "time": "2026-08-06T16:00",
    "temperature_2m": 71.4
  }
}

Take a second and let this land. Every single piece of what’s on your screen is something you already know:

  • The endpoint and the query string in the address bar (?, &, key-value pairs) — Session 2
  • The response wrapped in curly braces { } — the body, in JSON — Session 1
  • Data (temperature_2m: 71.4) and metadata (current_units, timezone) — Session 1
  • Your browser made a GET request — typing a URL into the address bar is always a GET — Session 2

That number — 71.4 — is the actual temperature in San Luis Obispo right now. A server you’ve never seen just measured the world and handed you the answer, because you asked correctly.

Now change latitude=35.28&longitude=-120.66 to another location (Boston is latitude=42.36&longitude=-71.06) and reload. Live data, different city, same endpoint. Edit the URL, press Enter, new answer — you are having a conversation with a server, by hand.

Important🎯 The Goal — Half Met Already

Read the goal sentence again: “Make a request to an API, then format the response into something we can analyze.”

  • Make a request to an API — ✅ you just did it. That URL was the request.
  • Get a response — ✅ you just did that too. That JSON was the response.

With zero lines of code, the request/response loop from Sessions 1 and 2 just happened for real, on your screen. So what’s left for R? Automation. The browser can make one request at a time, by hand, and you have to read the JSON with your eyes. R will do exactly the same thing the browser just did — same URL, same GET, same JSON — but it can do it a hundred times in a loop and hand the answers back as data you can analyze. That’s the entire rest of the workshop: not a new idea, just automating the thing you just did.

———————

Q3.

(Fill in the Blank): When you paste the request URL into a browser, what comes back is not a web page — it is raw ________.

TipAnswer Q3

JSON — the same body/content structure we studied in Session 1, Part 4.

———————

———————

Q4.

(Multiple Choice): Typing a URL into the browser’s address bar and pressing Enter performs which kind of HTTP request?

  1. POST
  2. DELETE
  3. PUT
  4. PATCH
  5. GET
TipAnswer Q4

e) The address bar always makes a GET request — you are reading data, exactly like our R scripts will.

———————

Part 3: The ETV Cycle — Our Map for the Rest of the Workshop

Everything we do from here on follows one repeating cycle — ETV:

Step Name What it means In code
E Extract Make the request, receive the JSON response request() → req_url_query() → req_perform()
T Transform Format the response into a data frame resp_body_json() → tibble()
V Visualize Turn the data frame into a plot ggplot()

We’ll do E and T in this session and add V in Session 4. Whenever you feel lost in code, ask: which ETV step am I on right now?

Load Libraries

Each library we load is hired for one specific ETV job. Read the comments as a map of the whole workshop:

library(httr2)       # E: makes web requests
library(tibble)      # T: tidyverse data frames
library(dplyr)       # T: data manipulation
library(purrr)       # T: map() — apply a recipe to many inputs
library(ggplot2)     # V: visualizations

The Functions Behind Each Letter

Here’s the deeper look — the specific functions each library gives us, and exactly where they sit in the cycle:

Library Key functions ETV step What it actually does
httr2 request(), req_url_query(), req_perform() E request() starts from the endpoint, req_url_query() builds the query string (the part after ?), and req_perform() actually sends it — together they do what your browser’s address bar did in Part 2
httr2 resp_status(), resp_body_json() E → T (the handoff) resp_status() checks for 200, and resp_body_json() unwraps the JSON body into an R named list — the bridge from response to data
tibble tibble(), tribble() T Builds the rectangular data frame — the “something we can analyze” from the goal sentence
dplyr bind_rows() T Stacks many small tibbles into one big one (we’ll need this the moment we ask about more than one city)
purrr map(), pmap() T (the multiplier) Applies the same E+T recipe to many inputs — this is the “automation” that makes R better than the browser
ggplot2 ggplot() V Turns the tibble into a plot — Session 4’s job

Notice the shape of that table: E is entirely httr2, T is tibble + dplyr + purrr, and V is ggplot2. When an error message mentions a function, the library it came from tells you which ETV step broke — that’s your debugging compass for the rest of the workshop.

Tip🎯 Goal Check

ETV is the goal sentence, written as three letters: E = make a request, T = format the response, V = analyze it. And the libraries are the goal sentence written as code: httr2 makes the request, tibble/dplyr/purrr format the response, ggplot2 analyzes it.

Part 4: Extract — The Browser Request, Now in R

Let’s have R do exactly what the browser just did. Two steps to build the request, one to send it:

# E is for Extract ------------------------------------------

# Step 1: Start from the endpoint and add the query
req <- request("https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast") |>
  req_url_query(
    latitude = 35.28,
    longitude = -120.66,
    current = "temperature_2m",
    temperature_unit = "fahrenheit"
  )

# Step 2: Look at the URL R built for us — same as the browser one!
req

# Step 3: Send the request
response <- req_perform(req)

# Step 4: Check the status code
resp_status(response)

The status should be 200 — success, just like Session 1 taught us to expect.

Notereq_url_query() Writes the URL for You

Each argument becomes one key=value pair in the query string, and httr2 handles the ?, the &, and any special-character encoding automatically. Printing req shows the finished URL — compare it character-by-character with the one you pasted into your browser.

# Step 5: Parse the JSON body into a named list
result <- resp_body_json(response)

# Step 6: Peek at the structure
str(result, max.level = 2)

———————

Q5.

(Fill in the Blank): After req_perform(), we call resp_status(response) and hope to see the number ________.

TipAnswer Q5

200 — the “OK” success code. Anything in the 4xx range would mean we made a mistake in the request; 5xx would mean the server had a problem.

———————

———————

Q6.

(Multiple Choice): What does req_url_query() do?

  1. It sends the request to the server.
  2. It parses the JSON response.
  3. It checks the status code.
  4. It adds key=value pairs to the URL’s query string, handling ?, &, and encoding for you.
  5. It draws a plot of the response.
TipAnswer Q6

d) req_url_query() builds the query string onto the endpoint. Sending is req_perform(), parsing is resp_body_json().

———————

Part 5: Transform — From JSON to a Data Frame

The parsed result is a named list (Session 1!). The piece we care about is result$current:

# T is for Transform ----------------------------------------

result$current

# Pull the values we want into a tibble
current_df <- tibble(
  city   = "San Luis Obispo",
  time   = result$current$time,
  temp_f = result$current$temperature_2m
)

current_df

That’s E and T — the entire workshop goal — in about ten lines.

Scaling Up: Many Cities with map()

What if we want several cities? We don’t need to copy-paste the code three times, and we don’t need to write our own function either. We give pmap() a recipe — an anonymous function, written \(...) — and it applies the recipe to every row of a small table:

# A small table of cities and their coordinates
cities <- tribble(
  ~city,             ~latitude, ~longitude,
  "San Luis Obispo",     35.28,    -120.66,
  "Boston",              42.36,     -71.06,
  "Ames",                42.03,     -93.62
)

# The recipe: for one row (one city), do E and T, return a one-row tibble
current_df <- cities |>
  pmap(\(city, latitude, longitude) {

    # E: extract
    result <- request("https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast") |>
      req_url_query(
        latitude = latitude,
        longitude = longitude,
        current = "temperature_2m",
        temperature_unit = "fahrenheit"
      ) |>
      req_perform() |>
      resp_body_json()

    # T: transform
    tibble(
      city   = city,
      time   = result$current$time,
      temp_f = result$current$temperature_2m
    )
  }) |>
  bind_rows()

current_df
NoteReading the map Pattern
  • \(city, latitude, longitude) { ... } is an anonymous function — a recipe with no name. The \( ) lists the ingredients; the { } holds the steps.
  • pmap() runs the recipe once per row of cities.
  • Each run returns a one-row tibble; bind_rows() stacks them into one data frame.

Same ETV steps as before — just repeated for us, without copy-paste and without defining named functions.

———————

Q7.

(Multiple Choice): In the code above, what does \(city, latitude, longitude) mean?

  1. It creates three new columns in the tibble.
  2. It is an anonymous function — a nameless recipe whose inputs are one row’s city, latitude, and longitude.
  3. It deletes the variables city, latitude, and longitude.
  4. It is a comment that R ignores.
  5. It is a file path.
TipAnswer Q7

b) \( ) is R’s shorthand for function( ). It defines a small nameless function on the spot, which pmap() then applies to every row.

———————

———————

Q8.

(Fill in the Blank): After pmap() returns a list of one-row tibbles, we stack them into a single data frame using ________.

TipAnswer Q8

bind_rows() — it binds the rows of each small tibble into one combined tibble.

———————

Part 6: Geocoding — Where Do the Coordinates Come From?

We typed the latitude and longitude by hand. But Open-Meteo also has a geocoding endpoint that converts a city name into coordinates.

Important⚠️ Look Closely — This Is a Different Endpoint

Compare the two front doors:

  • Forecast: https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast
  • Geocoding: https://geocoding-api.open-meteo.com/v1/search

Everything changed — different subdomain (geocoding-api vs. api), different path (/search vs. /forecast), and it will take different query parameters (name and count instead of latitude and longitude). Remember Part 1: each service gets its own machine door. Different endpoint = different service = different inputs and different response shape. Reading an endpoint’s requirements is a skill you’ll use with every API you ever touch.

Browser first, as always — and this time let’s use Boston as our example. Paste this:

https://geocoding-api.open-meteo.com/v1/search?name=Boston&count=1

You’ll see JSON with a results array whose first entry contains Boston’s latitude (about 42.36), longitude (about -71.06), population, and more. We asked a name question at a different door and got a coordinates answer — same request/response loop, brand-new service. Now the same thing in R — with map() and an anonymous function again:

city_names <- c("Boston", "San Luis Obispo", "Ames")

coords_df <- city_names |>
  map(\(nm) {

    # E: extract
    result <- request("https://geocoding-api.open-meteo.com/v1/search") |>
      req_url_query(name = nm, count = 1) |>
      req_perform() |>
      resp_body_json()

    # T: transform (first hit in the results array)
    hit <- result$results[[1]]
    tibble(
      city      = nm,
      latitude  = round(hit$latitude, 2),
      longitude = round(hit$longitude, 2)
    )
  }) |>
  bind_rows()

coords_df

Now we can find any city’s coordinates — which Session 4 will need, because the historical weather endpoint only speaks latitude/longitude (and Boston is one of the two cities Session 4 compares).

Tip🎯 Goal Check

Notice we just ran the same ETV pattern a third time — on a completely different endpoint, with different parameters and a different response shape — and none of our skills changed. That’s the whole trick: every API interaction, at every endpoint, at every company, is the same cycle.

———————

Q9.

(Fill in the Blank): The geocoding endpoint converts a city name into ________ and ________.

TipAnswer Q9

Latitude and longitude — the coordinates the forecast and historical endpoints require.

———————

Part 7: Your Turn — Build Your Own Request

Make a current weather request for your hometown (or any city you choose).

Activity: Fill in the Blanks

# Step 1: Find your city's coordinates with the geocoding endpoint
my_coords <- request("https://geocoding-api.open-meteo.com/v1/search") |>
  req_url_query(name = "________", count = 1) |>
  req_perform() |>
  resp_body_json()

my_lat <- my_coords$results[[1]]$________
my_lon <- my_coords$results[[1]]$________

# Step 2: Request the current weather (E)
my_result <- request("https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/________") |>
  req_url_query(
    latitude = ________,
    longitude = ________,
    current = "temperature_2m",
    temperature_unit = "fahrenheit"
  ) |>
  req_perform() |>
  resp_body_json()

# Step 3: Format the response into a tibble (T)
my_df <- tibble(
  city   = "________",
  time   = my_result$current$________,
  temp_f = my_result$current$________
)

my_df
TipSolution 
my_coords <- request("https://geocoding-api.open-meteo.com/v1/search") |>
  req_url_query(name = "Chicago", count = 1) |>
  req_perform() |>
  resp_body_json()

my_lat <- my_coords$results[[1]]$latitude
my_lon <- my_coords$results[[1]]$longitude

my_result <- request("https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast") |>
  req_url_query(
    latitude = my_lat,
    longitude = my_lon,
    current = "temperature_2m",
    temperature_unit = "fahrenheit"
  ) |>
  req_perform() |>
  resp_body_json()

my_df <- tibble(
  city   = "Chicago",
  time   = my_result$current$time,
  temp_f = my_result$current$temperature_2m
)

my_df

Q10.

(Ordering — from Session 2): Put the following steps in the correct order for making an API request in R. Write the letters in order.

  1. Parse the JSON response into a data frame
  2. Construct the URL with endpoint and query parameters
  3. Check the status code for success (200)
  4. Send the request using req_perform()
  5. Create a request object with request()
TipAnswer Q10

b → e → d → c → a

  1. b) Construct the URL with endpoint and query parameters
  2. e) Create a request object with request()
  3. d) Send the request using req_perform()
  4. c) Check the status code for success (200)
  5. a) Parse the JSON response into a data frame

(In practice, request() + req_url_query() do steps b and e together.)

———————

Session 3 Recap

Today the goal became real:

  1. Open-Meteo API — free, no API key, endpoint https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast
  2. Browser first — a request is just a URL; pasting it made a real request and the raw JSON on screen was a real response — the goal, met with zero code. R doesn’t do anything new; it automates what the browser did
  3. ETV Cycle — Extract (request), Transform (JSON → tibble), Visualize (Session 4) — with each library owning one letter: httr2 = E, tibble/dplyr/purrr = T, ggplot2 = V
  4. Extract in R — request() |> req_url_query() |> req_perform() |> resp_body_json()
  5. Transform in R — pulling values from the named list into a tibble()
  6. Scaling with map() — anonymous functions \( ) apply the same recipe to many cities, no copy-paste
  7. Geocoding — a different endpoint (geocoding-api.open-meteo.com/v1/search) that converts city names (like Boston) into the coordinates other endpoints need — different door, same ETV skills

Up next in Session 4: the V in ETV — historical weather data for Boston vs. San Luis Obispo, and your own visualizations!

## Part 2: See It in the Browser First — The Big Moment

**Stop. This is the moment the last two sessions have been building toward.**

For a day and a half, "request" and "response" have been arrows on a diagram. In the next sixty seconds they become *real* — and you will not write a single line of code to do it.

Here is the payoff of Session 2's URL anatomy: **a request is just a URL — so a web browser can make one.** Look at this URL *before* you paste it. You can already read every piece of it — that's Session 2:

```
https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=35.28&longitude=-120.66&current=temperature_2m&temperature_unit=fahrenheit
```

- `https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast` — the **endpoint** (the stable front door)
- `?` — "here come my details"
- `latitude=35.28&longitude=-120.66` — *where* (San Luis Obispo)
- `current=temperature_2m` — *what* (the temperature right now)
- `temperature_unit=fahrenheit` — *how* (in °F)

**You are literally looking at a request, written out as a URL.** Now copy it, paste it into a new browser tab, and press Enter.

**What just happened?** Your browser sent that request across the internet to Open-Meteo's server, and the server answered. What came back is not a web page — no colors, no buttons, no ads. It is a raw **JSON response**, exactly the structure we studied in Session 1, sitting right there in your browser:

``` json
{
  "latitude": 35.28,
  "longitude": -120.66,
  "timezone": "GMT",
  "current_units": { "time": "iso8601", "temperature_2m": "°F" },
  "current": {
    "time": "2026-08-06T16:00",
    "temperature_2m": 71.4
  }
}
```

Take a second and let this land. Every single piece of what's on your screen is something you already know:

- The **endpoint** and the **query string** in the address bar (`?`, `&`, key-value pairs) — *Session 2*
- The response wrapped in curly braces `{ }` — the **body**, in **JSON** — *Session 1*
- **Data** (`temperature_2m: 71.4`) and **metadata** (`current_units`, `timezone`) — *Session 1*
- Your browser made a **GET** request — typing a URL into the address bar is always a GET — *Session 2*

That number — `71.4` — is the actual temperature in San Luis Obispo *right now*. A server you've never seen just measured the world and handed you the answer, because you asked correctly.

Now change `latitude=35.28&longitude=-120.66` to another location (Boston is `latitude=42.36&longitude=-71.06`) and reload. Live data, different city, same endpoint. Edit the URL, press Enter, new answer — **you are having a conversation with a server, by hand.**

::: {.callout-important}
## 🎯 The Goal — Half Met Already

Read the goal sentence again: *"Make a request to an API, then format the response into something we can analyze."*

- **Make a request to an API** — ✅ you just did it. That URL *was* the request.
- **Get a response** — ✅ you just did that too. That JSON *was* the response.

With **zero lines of code**, the request/response loop from Sessions 1 and 2 just happened for real, on your screen. So what's left for R? **Automation.** The browser can make one request at a time, by hand, and you have to read the JSON with your eyes. R will do *exactly the same thing* the browser just did — same URL, same GET, same JSON — but it can do it a hundred times in a loop and hand the answers back as data you can analyze. That's the entire rest of the workshop: not a new idea, just automating the thing you just did.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer Q3"}

a) POST

## Part 3: The ETV Cycle — Our Map for the Rest of the Workshop

<!-- TODO(Immanuel): link/embed your ETV Cycle 4 notes here -->

Everything we do from here on follows one repeating cycle — **ETV**:

| Step | Name | What it means | In code |
|------|------|----------------|---------|
| **E** | **Extract** | Make the request, receive the JSON response | `request()` → `req_url_query()` → `req_perform()` |
| **T** | **Transform** | Format the response into a data frame | `resp_body_json()` → `tibble()` |
| **V** | **Visualize** | Turn the data frame into a plot | `ggplot()` |

We'll do **E** and **T** in this session and add **V** in Session 4. Whenever you feel lost in code, ask: *which ETV step am I on right now?*

### Load Libraries

Each library we load is hired for **one specific ETV job**. Read the comments as a map of the whole workshop:

```{r}
#| output: false
library(httr2)       # E: makes web requests
library(tibble)      # T: tidyverse data frames
library(dplyr)       # T: data manipulation
library(purrr)       # T: map() — apply a recipe to many inputs
library(ggplot2)     # V: visualizations
```

### The Functions Behind Each Letter

Here's the deeper look — the specific functions each library gives us, and exactly where they sit in the cycle:

| Library | Key functions | ETV step | What it actually does |
|---------|---------------|----------|------------------------|
| `httr2` | `request()`, `req_url_query()`, `req_perform()` | **E** | `request()` starts from the endpoint, `req_url_query()` builds the query string (the part after `?`), and `req_perform()` actually sends it — together they do what your browser's address bar did in Part 2 |
| `httr2` | `resp_status()`, `resp_body_json()` | **E → T** (the handoff) | `resp_status()` checks for `200`, and `resp_body_json()` unwraps the JSON body into an R named list — the bridge from *response* to *data* |
| `tibble` | `tibble()`, `tribble()` | **T** | Builds the rectangular data frame — the "something we can analyze" from the goal sentence |
| `dplyr` | `bind_rows()` | **T** | Stacks many small tibbles into one big one (we'll need this the moment we ask about more than one city) |
| `purrr` | `map()`, `pmap()` | **T** (the multiplier) | Applies the same E+T recipe to many inputs — this is the "automation" that makes R better than the browser |
| `ggplot2` | `ggplot()` | **V** | Turns the tibble into a plot — Session 4's job |

Notice the shape of that table: **E is entirely `httr2`**, **T is `tibble` + `dplyr` + `purrr`**, and **V is `ggplot2`**. When an error message mentions a function, the library it came from tells you *which ETV step broke* — that's your debugging compass for the rest of the workshop.

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🎯 Goal Check
ETV *is* the goal sentence, written as three letters: **E** = make a request, **T** = format the response, **V** = analyze it. And the libraries are the goal sentence written as code: `httr2` makes the request, `tibble`/`dplyr`/`purrr` format the response, `ggplot2` analyzes it.
:::


---


## Part 4: Extract — The Browser Request, Now in R

Let's have R do exactly what the browser just did. Two steps to build the request, one to send it:

```{r}
# E is for Extract ------------------------------------------

# Step 1: Start from the endpoint and add the query
req <- request("https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast") |>
  req_url_query(
    latitude = 35.28,
    longitude = -120.66,
    current = "temperature_2m",
    temperature_unit = "fahrenheit"
  )

# Step 2: Look at the URL R built for us — same as the browser one!
req

# Step 3: Send the request
response <- req_perform(req)

# Step 4: Check the status code
resp_status(response)
```

The status should be `200` — success, just like Session 1 taught us to expect.

::: {.callout-note}
## `req_url_query()` Writes the URL for You
Each argument becomes one `key=value` pair in the query string, and `httr2` handles the `?`, the `&`, and any special-character encoding automatically. Printing `req` shows the finished URL — compare it character-by-character with the one you pasted into your browser.
:::

```{r}
# Step 5: Parse the JSON body into a named list
result <- resp_body_json(response)

# Step 6: Peek at the structure
str(result, max.level = 2)
```


#### ———————
### Q5. {.unnumbered}

**(Fill in the Blank):** After `req_perform()`, we call `resp_status(response)` and hope to see the number \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer Q5"}
**200** — the "OK" success code. Anything in the 4xx range would mean *we* made a mistake in the request; 5xx would mean the server had a problem.
:::
#### ———————


#### ———————
### Q6. {.unnumbered}

**(Multiple Choice):** What does `req_url_query()` do?

a) It sends the request to the server.
b) It parses the JSON response.
c) It checks the status code.
d) It adds `key=value` pairs to the URL's query string, handling `?`, `&`, and encoding for you.
e) It draws a plot of the response.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer Q6"}
**d)** `req_url_query()` *builds* the query string onto the endpoint. Sending is `req_perform()`, parsing is `resp_body_json()`.
:::
#### ———————


---


## Part 5: Transform — From JSON to a Data Frame

The parsed `result` is a **named list** (Session 1!). The piece we care about is `result$current`:

```{r}
# T is for Transform ----------------------------------------

result$current

# Pull the values we want into a tibble
current_df <- tibble(
  city   = "San Luis Obispo",
  time   = result$current$time,
  temp_f = result$current$temperature_2m
)

current_df
```

That's **E** and **T** — the entire workshop goal — in about ten lines.

### Scaling Up: Many Cities with `map()`

What if we want **several cities**? We don't need to copy-paste the code three times, and we don't need to write our own function either. We give `pmap()` a *recipe* — an **anonymous function**, written `\(...)` — and it applies the recipe to every row of a small table:

```{r}
# A small table of cities and their coordinates
cities <- tribble(
  ~city,             ~latitude, ~longitude,
  "San Luis Obispo",     35.28,    -120.66,
  "Boston",              42.36,     -71.06,
  "Ames",                42.03,     -93.62
)

# The recipe: for one row (one city), do E and T, return a one-row tibble
current_df <- cities |>
  pmap(\(city, latitude, longitude) {

    # E: extract
    result <- request("https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast") |>
      req_url_query(
        latitude = latitude,
        longitude = longitude,
        current = "temperature_2m",
        temperature_unit = "fahrenheit"
      ) |>
      req_perform() |>
      resp_body_json()

    # T: transform
    tibble(
      city   = city,
      time   = result$current$time,
      temp_f = result$current$temperature_2m
    )
  }) |>
  bind_rows()

current_df
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Reading the `map` Pattern

- `\(city, latitude, longitude) { ... }` is an **anonymous function** — a recipe with no name. The `\( )` lists the ingredients; the `{ }` holds the steps.
- `pmap()` runs the recipe once **per row** of `cities`.
- Each run returns a one-row tibble; `bind_rows()` stacks them into one data frame.

Same ETV steps as before — just repeated for us, without copy-paste and without defining named functions.
:::


#### ———————
### Q7. {.unnumbered}

**(Multiple Choice):** In the code above, what does `\(city, latitude, longitude)` mean?

a) It creates three new columns in the tibble.
b) It is an anonymous function — a nameless recipe whose inputs are one row's city, latitude, and longitude.
c) It deletes the variables city, latitude, and longitude.
d) It is a comment that R ignores.
e) It is a file path.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer Q7"}
**b)** `\( )` is R's shorthand for `function( )`. It defines a small nameless function on the spot, which `pmap()` then applies to every row.
:::
#### ———————


#### ———————
### Q8. {.unnumbered}

**(Fill in the Blank):** After `pmap()` returns a list of one-row tibbles, we stack them into a single data frame using \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer Q8"}
`bind_rows()` — it binds the rows of each small tibble into one combined tibble.
:::

## Part 6: Geocoding — Where Do the Coordinates Come From?

We typed the latitude and longitude by hand. But Open-Meteo also has a **geocoding** endpoint that converts a city *name* into coordinates.

::: {.callout-important}
## ⚠️ Look Closely — This Is a *Different Endpoint*

Compare the two front doors:

- Forecast: `https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast`
- Geocoding: `https://geocoding-api.open-meteo.com/v1/search`

**Everything changed** — different subdomain (`geocoding-api` vs. `api`), different path (`/search` vs. `/forecast`), and it will take different query parameters (`name` and `count` instead of `latitude` and `longitude`). Remember Part 1: each service gets its own machine door. Different endpoint = different service = different inputs and different response shape. Reading an endpoint's requirements is a skill you'll use with *every* API you ever touch.
:::

Browser first, as always — and this time let's use **Boston** as our example. Paste this:

```
https://geocoding-api.open-meteo.com/v1/search?name=Boston&count=1
```

You'll see JSON with a `results` array whose first entry contains Boston's `latitude` (about 42.36), `longitude` (about -71.06), `population`, and more. We asked a *name* question at a *different door* and got a *coordinates* answer — same request/response loop, brand-new service. Now the same thing in R — with `map()` and an anonymous function again:

```{r}
city_names <- c("Boston", "San Luis Obispo", "Ames")

coords_df <- city_names |>
  map(\(nm) {

    # E: extract
    result <- request("https://geocoding-api.open-meteo.com/v1/search") |>
      req_url_query(name = nm, count = 1) |>
      req_perform() |>
      resp_body_json()

    # T: transform (first hit in the results array)
    hit <- result$results[[1]]
    tibble(
      city      = nm,
      latitude  = round(hit$latitude, 2),
      longitude = round(hit$longitude, 2)
    )
  }) |>
  bind_rows()

coords_df
```

Now we can find *any* city's coordinates — which Session 4 will need, because the historical weather endpoint only speaks latitude/longitude (and Boston is one of the two cities Session 4 compares).

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🎯 Goal Check
Notice we just ran the **same ETV pattern a third time** — on a **completely different endpoint**, with different parameters and a different response shape — and none of our skills changed. That's the whole trick: every API interaction, at every endpoint, at every company, is the same cycle.
:::


#### ———————
### Q9. {.unnumbered}

**(Fill in the Blank):** The geocoding endpoint converts a city name into \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ and \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer Q9"}
**Latitude** and **longitude** — the coordinates the forecast and historical endpoints require.
:::

## Part 7: Your Turn — Build Your Own Request

Make a current weather request for **your hometown** (or any city you choose).

### Activity: Fill in the Blanks

```{r}
# Step 1: Find your city's coordinates with the geocoding endpoint
my_coords <- request("https://geocoding-api.open-meteo.com/v1/search") |>
  req_url_query(name = "________", count = 1) |>
  req_perform() |>
  resp_body_json()

my_lat <- my_coords$results[[1]]$________
my_lon <- my_coords$results[[1]]$________

# Step 2: Request the current weather (E)
my_result <- request("https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/________") |>
  req_url_query(
    latitude = ________,
    longitude = ________,
    current = "temperature_2m",
    temperature_unit = "fahrenheit"
  ) |>
  req_perform() |>
  resp_body_json()

# Step 3: Format the response into a tibble (T)
my_df <- tibble(
  city   = "________",
  time   = my_result$current$________,
  temp_f = my_result$current$________
)

my_df
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```{r}
my_coords <- request("https://geocoding-api.open-meteo.com/v1/search") |>
  req_url_query(name = "Chicago", count = 1) |>
  req_perform() |>
  resp_body_json()

my_lat <- my_coords$results[[1]]$latitude
my_lon <- my_coords$results[[1]]$longitude

my_result <- request("https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast") |>
  req_url_query(
    latitude = my_lat,
    longitude = my_lon,
    current = "temperature_2m",
    temperature_unit = "fahrenheit"
  ) |>
  req_perform() |>
  resp_body_json()

my_df <- tibble(
  city   = "Chicago",
  time   = my_result$current$time,
  temp_f = my_result$current$temperature_2m
)

my_df
```
:::

### Q10. {.unnumbered}

**(Ordering — from Session 2):** Put the following steps in the correct order for making an API request in R. Write the letters in order.

a) Parse the JSON response into a data frame
b) Construct the URL with endpoint and query parameters
c) Check the status code for success (200)
d) Send the request using `req_perform()`
e) Create a request object with `request()`

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer Q10"}
**b → e → d → c → a**

1. **b)** Construct the URL with endpoint and query parameters
2. **e)** Create a request object with `request()`
3. **d)** Send the request using `req_perform()`
4. **c)** Check the status code for success (200)
5. **a)** Parse the JSON response into a data frame

(In practice, `request()` + `req_url_query()` do steps b and e together.)
:::

## Session 3 Recap

Today the goal became real:

1. **Open-Meteo API** — free, no API key, endpoint `https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast`
2. **Browser first** — a request is just a URL; pasting it made a real request and the raw JSON on screen was a real response — the goal, met with zero code. R doesn't do anything new; it **automates** what the browser did
3. **ETV Cycle** — Extract (request), Transform (JSON → tibble), Visualize (Session 4) — with each library owning one letter: `httr2` = E, `tibble`/`dplyr`/`purrr` = T, `ggplot2` = V
4. **Extract in R** — `request()` |> `req_url_query()` |> `req_perform()` |> `resp_body_json()`
5. **Transform in R** — pulling values from the named list into a `tibble()`
6. **Scaling with `map()`** — anonymous functions `\( )` apply the same recipe to many cities, no copy-paste
7. **Geocoding** — a **different endpoint** (`geocoding-api.open-meteo.com/v1/search`) that converts city names (like Boston) into the coordinates other endpoints need — different door, same ETV skills

**Up next in Session 4:** the **V** in ETV — historical weather data for Boston vs. San Luis Obispo, and your own visualizations!
